claims.text: Prolonged high-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by selective oxidation of reactive elements.
Oxidizing environments rapidly produce an adherent Al- and Cr-enriched oxide scale.
An Al- and Cr-enriched oxide scale protects the underlying fcc matrix by limiting oxygen penetration.
Reducing atmospheres prevent formation of a stable protective scale.
The absence of a protective scale under reducing conditions permits preferential Ti oxidation.
Reducing conditions accelerate coarsening of nascent precipitates near grain boundaries.
Ti oxidation and precipitate coarsening compromise the alloy's mechanical performance.
The starting material has the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 composition.
The as-built alloy has a predominantly fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains minimal pre-existing secondary phases.
Aging near 750 degrees Celsius is an applicable condition for studying matrix and gamma-prime precipitate evolution in this alloy system.
The cited alloy system exhibits time-dependent evolution of its matrix and gamma-prime precipitates during aging at 750 degrees Celsius.
Oxidizing treatment will preserve the fcc matrix and retain mechanical properties relative to the baseline.
Reducing treatment will cause more Ti oxidation, grain-boundary precipitate coarsening, and mechanical degradation than the baseline.
The as-built baseline has known high strength and fatigue performance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply around 750 degrees Celsius under clearly oxidizing or reducing gas chemistries.
Mixed oxidation states or temperatures outside the proposed range could produce ambiguous results.
Comparable specimens exposed for 10, 25, and 50 hours in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres can distinguish the proposed mechanism through oxide, microstructural, and mechanical measurements.
